## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Explain why a package is the best home for functions you reuse.
2. Describe the files and folders in a package, and what each one does.
3. Document functions with roxygen2 comments.
4. Write unit tests with testthat.
5. Build, check and install a package with devtools.

::: {.callout-important}
## Part of today runs on your own computer
Creating, building and checking a package needs R and RStudio on your computer. Follow the [setup guide](../setup.qmd), then install the tools once:

```r
install.packages(c("devtools", "usethis", "roxygen2", "testthat"))
```

You can do the exercises here in the browser. They cover the parts you write by hand: tests, documentation comments and the `DESCRIPTION` file.
:::

```{webr}
library(testthat)
```

## Why write a package?

Once you have functions you use in more than one project, copying a `helpers.R` file between folders stops working. Copies drift apart, bugs get fixed in one place but not another, and nobody remembers which version is current.

A **package** solves this. It gives your functions:

- **one home**, installed once and loaded with `library()`;
- **documentation**, so `?your_function` works for you and your colleagues;
- **tests** that run with one command and tell you when a change breaks something;
- **a version number**, so you know which code produced which result;
- **an easy way to share**, through GitHub or CRAN.

A package does not have to be public or polished. A small package for your team's cleaning functions is a very good use of one.

## The structure of a package

A package is a folder with a fixed layout:

```
surveytools/
├── DESCRIPTION        what the package is, who wrote it, what it needs
├── NAMESPACE          which functions are exported (written for you by roxygen2)
├── LICENSE            the licence (added by usethis)
├── R/                 your functions, in .R files
│   ├── clean.R
│   └── summarise.R
├── man/               help pages (written for you by roxygen2)
├── tests/
│   ├── testthat.R
│   └── testthat/      your tests
│       └── test-clean.R
└── README.md          what a visitor sees first on GitHub
```

You write `DESCRIPTION`, the files in `R/` and the files in `tests/testthat/`. Tools generate most of the rest.

### `DESCRIPTION`

`DESCRIPTION` is a text file of `Field: value` lines:

```
Package: surveytools
Title: Clean and Summarise Household Survey Data
Version: 0.1.0
Authors@R: person("Ada", "Lovelace", email = "ada@example.org", role = c("aut", "cre"))
Description: Functions to standardise household IDs, validate survey
    data and produce district summaries.
License: MIT + file LICENSE
Encoding: UTF-8
Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
RoxygenNote: 7.3.2
Imports:
    dplyr,
    stringr
Suggests:
    testthat (>= 3.0.0)
Config/testthat/edition: 3
```

- **Package** may contain only letters, numbers and dots, and must start with a letter.
- **Title** is one line in title case, without a full stop.
- **Version** usually starts at `0.1.0`. Increase it when you release changes.
- **Imports** lists packages your functions need. They are installed with yours.
- **Suggests** lists packages needed only for tests or examples.

You can read a `DESCRIPTION` file in R with `read.dcf()`:

```{webr}
desc_text <- "Package: surveytools
Title: Clean and Summarise Household Survey Data
Version: 0.1.0
Imports: dplyr, stringr"

desc <- read.dcf(textConnection(desc_text))
desc[, "Package"]
desc[, "Imports"]
```

## The package workflow

::: {.callout-important}
## Run this on your own computer
**1. Create the package.** In the RStudio Console:

```r
usethis::create_package("~/projects/surveytools")
```

A new RStudio session opens in the package folder.

**2. Add a licence and a first function file:**

```r
usethis::use_mit_license()
usethis::use_r("clean")        # creates and opens R/clean.R
```

**3. Write your function in `R/clean.R`**, with roxygen2 comments above it (see the next section).

**4. Load it and try it.** `load_all()` loads every function in `R/` as if the package were installed. Run it every time you change the code (shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+L, or Cmd+Shift+L on a Mac):

```r
devtools::load_all()
clean_id(" hh1 ")
```

**5. Generate the documentation:**

```r
devtools::document()           # writes man/ and NAMESPACE from your comments
?clean_id                      # your help page
```

**6. Add tests:**

```r
usethis::use_testthat()        # once per package
usethis::use_test("clean")     # creates tests/testthat/test-clean.R
devtools::test()               # runs all tests
```

**7. Declare the packages you use:**

```r
usethis::use_package("stringr")   # adds stringr to Imports in DESCRIPTION
```

Then call its functions as `stringr::str_pad()` inside your package. Do **not** put `library()` calls in package code.

**8. Check the whole package:**

```r
devtools::check()
```

`check()` runs R's full set of package checks: it builds the package, runs the tests and examples, and looks for missing documentation and undeclared dependencies. Aim for **0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes**.

**9. Install it and share it:**

```r
devtools::install()                          # install on your computer
# after pushing the folder to GitHub:
# remotes::install_github("your-name/surveytools")
```
:::

The cycle you will repeat most is: **edit, `load_all()`, try, test**.

## Documentation with roxygen2

**roxygen2** turns special comments, starting with `#'`, into help pages. You write them directly above each function:

```r
#' Standardise household IDs
#'
#' Removes spaces, converts to upper case and pads the number to three
#' digits, so " hh1 " becomes "HH001".
#'
#' @param x A character vector of household IDs.
#' @param width Number of digits in the padded number.
#'
#' @return A character vector the same length as `x`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' clean_id(c(" hh1 ", "HH 25"))
clean_id <- function(x, width = 3) {
  number <- stringr::str_extract(x, "\\d+")
  paste0("HH", stringr::str_pad(number, width = width, pad = "0"))
}
```

| Tag | Means |
|---|---|
| first line | the title of the help page |
| next paragraph | the description |
| `@param name` | one per argument: what it is |
| `@return` | what the function returns |
| `@export` | make the function available to users after `library()` |
| `@examples` | code that runs when someone calls `example()`, and during `check()` |

Functions without `@export` are **internal**: your other functions can use them, but users do not see them. Keep helpers internal so you are free to change them.

## Tests with testthat

A **unit test** runs a function on a known input and checks the output. Tests catch the bugs you would otherwise find months later in a report.

### Expectations

An **expectation** checks one thing. It does nothing if the check passes and gives an error if it fails:

```{webr}
expect_equal(round(2.567, 1), 2.6)          # passes silently
expect_true(is.numeric(42))
expect_length(1:3, 3)
expect_error(log("a"))                       # passes: log("a") does give an error
```

```{webr}
expect_equal(round(2.567, 1), 2.5) # Error expected: the expectation fails
```

The expectations you will use most:

| Expectation | Checks that… |
|---|---|
| `expect_equal(x, y)` | `x` equals `y`, allowing for tiny rounding differences |
| `expect_identical(x, y)` | `x` is exactly `y`, including type |
| `expect_true(x)`, `expect_false(x)` | `x` is `TRUE` or `FALSE` |
| `expect_error(code)` | the code gives an error. Add a pattern to check the message: `expect_error(code, "must be numeric")` |
| `expect_warning(code)` | the code gives a warning |
| `expect_length(x, n)` | `x` has `n` elements |
| `expect_type(x, "character")` | `x` has that type |

### `test_that()`

Group related expectations into a test with a short description of the behaviour:

```{webr}
clean_id <- function(x, width = 3) {
  number <- regmatches(x, regexpr("[0-9]+", x))
  paste0("HH", formatC(as.integer(number), width = width, flag = "0"))
}

test_that("clean_id() standardises IDs", {
  expect_equal(clean_id(" hh1 "), "HH001")
  expect_equal(clean_id("HH 25"), "HH025")
  expect_length(clean_id(c("hh1", "hh2")), 2)
})
```

In a package, tests live in files such as `tests/testthat/test-clean.R`, and `devtools::test()` runs them all and prints a summary.

### What to test

- **Typical inputs**: the cases you wrote the function for.
- **Edge cases**: an empty vector, a single value, `NA`, very large numbers.
- **Errors**: bad input should fail with the message you wrote (Day 16).
- **Every bug you fix.** Write a test that fails because of the bug, then fix the code. The bug can never come back unnoticed.

```{webr}
percent <- function(part, total) {
  if (!is.numeric(part) || !is.numeric(total)) stop("`part` and `total` must be numeric.")
  100 * part / total
}

test_that("percent() works and fails clearly", {
  expect_equal(percent(1, 4), 25)
  expect_equal(percent(c(1, 2), 4), c(25, 50))
  expect_true(is.na(percent(NA_real_, 4)))
  expect_error(percent("1", 4), "must be numeric")
})
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Write the test first
Some programmers write the test **before** the function. It forces you to decide exactly what the function should do, and you know you are finished when the test passes. This is called test-driven development.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
In a spreadsheet, you might check a total by adding it up a second way in a cell off to the side. Tests are those check cells, written down once and run every time anything changes.
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Write a `DESCRIPTION`

Complete the `DESCRIPTION` text for a package called `cropstats`, with the title `Summarise Crop Yields`, version `0.1.0` and `MIT + file LICENSE` as the licence.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_desc
desc_text <- "Package: ______
Title: ______
Version: ______
License: ______"
read.dcf(textConnection(desc_text))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex20_desc"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Each line is `Field: value`, with no quotes around the value: for example `Package: cropstats`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex20_desc"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
desc_text <- "Package: cropstats
Title: Summarise Crop Yields
Version: 0.1.0
License: MIT + file LICENSE"
read.dcf(textConnection(desc_text))
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_desc
#| check: true
d <- tryCatch(read.dcf(textConnection(desc_text)), error = function(e) NULL)
field <- function(f) if (!is.null(d) && f %in% colnames(d)) unname(d[1, f]) else NA_character_
if (is.null(d)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The text cannot be read. Each line should be Field: value.")
} else if (grepl("\"", paste(d, collapse = ""))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Remove the quotes. DESCRIPTION values are written without them.")
} else if (!identical(field("Package"), "cropstats")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Package should be cropstats.")
} else if (!identical(field("Title"), "Summarise Crop Yields")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Title should be Summarise Crop Yields.")
} else if (!identical(field("Version"), "0.1.0")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Version should be 0.1.0.")
} else if (!identical(field("License"), "MIT + file LICENSE")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "License should be MIT + file LICENSE.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. That is a valid start to a DESCRIPTION file.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Document a function

Write roxygen2 comments for `yield_per_acre()`. Include a title, an `@param` line for **each** argument, a `@return` line and `@export`. Save the comment lines as the character vector `doc`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_roxygen
yield_per_acre <- function(yield_kg, acres) yield_kg / acres

doc <- c(
  "#' Yield per acre",
  "#'",
  "#' @param yield_kg ______",
  "#' @param ______ Area planted, in acres.",
  "#' @return ______",
  "#' ______"
)
cat(doc, sep = "\n")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex20_roxygen"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Describe `yield_kg` in a few words, add `@param acres`, describe the result after `@return`, and make the last line `#' @export`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex20_roxygen"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
yield_per_acre <- function(yield_kg, acres) yield_kg / acres

doc <- c(
  "#' Yield per acre",
  "#'",
  "#' @param yield_kg Total harvest, in kilograms.",
  "#' @param acres Area planted, in acres.",
  "#' @return A number: kilograms per acre.",
  "#' @export"
)
cat(doc, sep = "\n")
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_roxygen
#| check: true
if (!exists("doc") || !is.character(doc)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the comment lines as the character vector doc.")
} else if (any(grepl("______", doc, fixed = TRUE))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Fill in every blank.")
} else if (!all(startsWith(doc, "#'"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Every roxygen2 line starts with #' (a hash and an apostrophe).")
} else {
  params <- sub("^#'\\s*@param\\s+(\\S+).*$", "\\1", grep("@param", doc, value = TRUE))
  if (!setequal(params, names(formals(yield_per_acre)))) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "There should be one @param line for each argument: yield_kg and acres.")
  } else if (any(grepl("^#'\\s*@param\\s+\\S+\\s*$", doc))) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "Each @param needs a description after the argument name.")
  } else if (!any(grepl("^#'\\s*@return\\s+\\S", doc))) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "Describe the result after @return.")
  } else if (!any(grepl("^#'\\s*@export\\s*$", doc))) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "Add #' @export so users can call the function.")
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. devtools::document() would turn this into a help page.")
  }
}
```

### Exercise 3: Write expectations

Write a `test_that()` block for `to_celsius()` with **two** expectations: `to_celsius(212)` equals `100`, and `to_celsius("hot")` gives an error.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_expect
#| setup: true
library(testthat)
to_celsius <- function(f) {
  if (!is.numeric(f)) stop("`f` must be numeric.")
  (f - 32) * 5 / 9
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_expect
test_that("to_celsius() converts and validates", {
  ______(to_celsius(212), 100)
  ______(to_celsius("hot"))
})
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex20_expect"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Use `expect_equal()` for the first and `expect_error()` for the second.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex20_expect"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
test_that("to_celsius() converts and validates", {
  expect_equal(to_celsius(212), 100)
  expect_error(to_celsius("hot"))
})
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_expect
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(.result)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Both expectations passed.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The test did not pass. Use expect_equal(to_celsius(212), 100) and expect_error(to_celsius(\"hot\")).")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Fix the code to pass the tests

These tests describe what `clean_district()` should do, but the function has a bug: it does not remove spaces. Fix the function so that all the tests pass when you run `run_tests(clean_district)`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_fix
#| setup: true
library(testthat)
run_tests <- function(clean_district) {
  expect_equal(clean_district("gulu"), "Gulu")
  expect_equal(clean_district("  ARUA "), "Arua")
  expect_equal(clean_district("mbale  town"), "Mbale Town")
  "all tests passed"
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_fix
clean_district <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  x <- gsub("\\b([a-z])", "\\U\\1", x, perl = TRUE)   # capitalise each word
  x
}
run_tests(clean_district)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex20_fix"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Add a line that removes extra spaces: `x <- trimws(gsub(" +", " ", x))` replaces runs of spaces with one space and trims the ends.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex20_fix"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
clean_district <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  x <- trimws(gsub(" +", " ", x))
  x <- gsub("\\b([a-z])", "\\U\\1", x, perl = TRUE)   # capitalise each word
  x
}
run_tests(clean_district)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_fix
#| check: true
res <- tryCatch(run_tests(clean_district), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
if (identical(res, "all tests passed")) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. The tests told you exactly when the bug was fixed.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = paste("A test still fails:", res))
}
```

### Exercise 5: Write a test that catches a bug

A good test **fails** when the code is wrong. Write `check_mean_size(f)`: it takes a function `f` and uses `expect_equal()` to check that `f(c(2, 4, NA))` equals `3`. The correct version of the function ignores `NA`. The buggy version does not.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_catch
#| setup: true
library(testthat)
good_mean <- function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
buggy_mean <- function(x) mean(x)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_catch
check_mean_size <- function(f) {
  ______(f(c(2, 4, NA)), ______)
}
check_mean_size(good_mean)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex20_catch"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Inside the function: `expect_equal(f(c(2, 4, NA)), 3)`. Try `check_mean_size(buggy_mean)` afterwards: it should fail.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex20_catch"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
check_mean_size <- function(f) {
  expect_equal(f(c(2, 4, NA)), 3)
}
check_mean_size(good_mean)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex20_catch
#| check: true
passes_good <- tryCatch({ check_mean_size(good_mean); TRUE }, error = function(e) FALSE)
catches_bug <- tryCatch({ check_mean_size(buggy_mean); FALSE }, error = function(e) TRUE)
if (!exists("check_mean_size") || !is.function(check_mean_size)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create a function called check_mean_size.")
} else if (!passes_good) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The test fails on the correct function. good_mean(c(2, 4, NA)) is 3.")
} else if (!catches_bug) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The test passes on the buggy function too, so it would not catch the bug. Check against the value 3.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Your test passes on good code and fails on buggy code, which is exactly what a test is for.")
}
```

Do this on your own computer.

1. Create a package called `surveytools` with `usethis::create_package()`.
2. Move two functions you wrote on Days 10 and 16 into `R/`. Document them with roxygen2, run `devtools::document()` and check that `?your_function` works.
3. Add a test file for each function with at least three expectations, including one `expect_error()`. Run `devtools::test()`.
4. Run `devtools::check()` and fix every error, warning and note.

You can practise tests here first:

```{webr}
library(testthat)
# Your code here

```

## Common mistakes

- **Using `library()` inside package code.** Declare the dependency with `usethis::use_package()` and call functions as `pkg::fun()`.
- **Editing `NAMESPACE` or files in `man/` by hand.** roxygen2 overwrites them. Change the `#'` comments and run `devtools::document()`.
- **Forgetting `@export`.** The function then works with `load_all()` but is missing after `library()`.
- **Tests that cannot fail.** `expect_true(TRUE)` always passes. Check that each test fails when the code is wrong.
- **Testing only the happy path.** Include edge cases and bad input.
- **Ignoring notes from `check()`.** They often point to real problems, such as an undeclared dependency.

## Summary

- A package gives reusable functions one home, with documentation, tests, a version and an easy way to share them.
- A package has `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, `R/`, `man/` and `tests/testthat/`. You write `DESCRIPTION`, `R/` and the tests.
- usethis creates files (`create_package()`, `use_r()`, `use_test()`, `use_package()`). devtools runs the workflow (`load_all()`, `document()`, `test()`, `check()`, `install()`).
- roxygen2 comments (`#'`) with `@param`, `@return`, `@export` and `@examples` become help pages.
- testthat expectations such as `expect_equal()` and `expect_error()` go inside `test_that()` blocks. Test typical cases, edge cases, errors and every bug you fix.

**Next:** Day 21 is the capstone project, where you use everything from the course on one dataset.
